Critics: Trump’s Netanyahu Endorsement Imperils GOP Election Chances, Meddles in Israeli Politics, and Harms Israel
U.S. President Donald Trump’s full-throated endorsement of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu didn’t just jeopardize the electoral hopes of Republican lawmakers in competitive seats, theorizes former U.S. counterterrorism chief Joe Kent.
The endorsement also directly meddles in Israel’s internal politics by telling the Israelis that the United States might not continue the war against Iran — supposedly crucial to Israel’s survival — if they vote against the prime minister. And that is “dangerous” for Israel, a writer for Haaretz concluded.
Which in turn means that Trump has turned the admonition of his primordial predecessor, George Washington, on its head. The first president warned against America’s entangling itself in the disputes of other nations. Trump has rushed headlong into one of those disputes.
From “Crazy” to “Great Warrior”
Trump’s unreserved endorsement, Haaretz writer Esther Solomon observed, comes after his summertime attack when he called Netanyahu “crazy.”
Trump was furious about Israel’s military operations in Lebanon.
Citing inside sources, Axios spilled the beans about a phone call between the two.
“Two of the sources said Trump claimed he’d helped keep Netanyahu out of jail — a reference to his support during Netanyahu’s corruption trial,” Axios reported:
Summarizing Trump’s remarks to Netanyahu, the U.S. official said: “You’re f**king crazy. You’d be in prison if it weren’t for me. I’m saving your a**. Everybody hates you now. Everybody hates Israel because of this.”
A second source briefed on the call said Trump was “p**sed” and at one point yelled at Netanyahu: “What the f**k are you doing?”
But yesterday, Trump warbled a new tune. Netanyahu might be the greatest prime minister in the annals of prime ministers.
Addressing the “great people of Israel” directly, Trump wrote that “Bibi Netanyahu has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran, with its 51 year old chant, ‘Death to Israel, Death to America! We will destroy the Little Satan and the Big Satan.’”
Then Trump bluntly told the Israelis they better re-elect his buddy “Bibi” … or else the United States will abandon Israel to Iran’s depredations:
Unless [Iran changes its] ways, rapidly, we will soon finish the job. If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so.
Netanyahu is “Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” Trump continued. And while “normal men” would collapse under such “pressure,” “Bibi did not wilt, he actually got stronger, and maintains that same Strength today.”
“Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel. BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!” Trump concluded.
Bibi was just as effusive in his reply. He was “so honored and humbled” by an endorsement from his “dear friend, Donald.” Trump, he said, is “laser focused” on ensuring that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon.
“Let me say to the American people,” Netanyahu said:
If you’re worried about today’s gas prices, think of what will happen if Iran gets nuclear weapons, something that Donald Trump and I will never allow. And when that happens, when that threat of that regime disappears, gas prices will go down — and how. But only under Trump. It’s not going to happen with those who want to accommodate and appease these tyrants, these butchers. I have to say that the world has been fortunate, America has been fortunate, America’s allies have been fortunate, Israel has been fortunate, and the Jewish people have been fortunate to have a leader of such clarity, consistency, conviction, and courage as Donald J. Trump.
Dangerous for Israel and the GOP
Trump has been a Netanyahu camp follower for years, Solomon wrote, and his endorsement won’t end in a majority vote for the prime minister because “no amount of flowery presidential language will budge” voters infuriated with Netanyahu’s policies.
But Solomon also targeted Trump’s threat: If Netanyahu loses, no more war with Iran.
“Trump’s endorsement was wrapped in a threat — if Israelis don’t vote for Netanyahu, then the president would ‘not [be] inclined’ to ‘finish the job’ with Iran,” she wrote:
Not only has Netanyahu legitimized an unprecedented act of interference in Israel’s internal affairs, but for the sake of that support, he has tethered Israel to an imminent, explicitly politically motivated, round of conflict with Iran.
Kent said much the same thing to X podcaster Mario Nawfal.
Wondering how much control the “pro-Israel lobby” and Netanyahu have over Trump, Kent called Trump’s endorsement “political suicide.” It will “hurt every single Republican” whom Trump endorsed, including those in red states — and particularly those in purple states where every vote counts. “This does not help anybody on the Republican ticket that is trying to get across the finish line,” he said.
“Every single Democrat out there that’s running against a Republican in a competitive seat is going to use this to show that, like, look … the Republican party is not taking orders from the American people, they’re taking [them] from Benjamin Netanyahu,” Kent said.
The endorsement raises one of the “the biggest questions of our time,” Kent continued. “Why did we get into this war? Why is President Trump doing all of these things that are against his base?”
But he also said what Solomon did. Trump has told the Israelis that “if you guys don’t elect Bibi, then I’m not really inclined to finish the Iran war,” Kent said. It’s “almost telling the Israelis … you’re kind of on your own unless you give me my guy.”
George Washington’s Admonition Turned on Its Head
Trump’s endorsement reverses George Washington’s warnings. “The great rule of conduct for us, in regard to foreign Nations is in extending our commercial relations to have with them as little political connection as possible,” he said in his farewell address of September 19, 1796:
So far as we have already formed engagements let them be fulfilled with perfect good faith. Here let us stop. … ’Tis our true policy to steer clear of permanent Alliances, with any portion of the foreign world.

The support for Netanyahu comes as Netanyahu is being accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

Contrary to what Trump claims, it is Netanyahu who urged him to launch war against Iran with the participation of Israel.
Joe Kent, former U.S. counterterrorism chief, resigned on March 17, 2026, in protest against the war. In his resignation letter, he stated that the United States had started the war “due to pressure from Israel and its powerful American lobby.” He also accused senior Israeli officials and influential media figures of promoting misinformation to encourage military action.
Also, Badr Albusaidi, Oman's foreign minister, explicitly said that Israel's leadership persuaded Trump to enter the war by presenting the prospect of a swift Iranian surrender. In a March 19, 2026 article in the Guardian, he said Washington's greatest miscalculation was allowing itself to be drawn into the conflict.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said on March 2, just three days after Iran came under unprovoked and illegal joint aggression, that Israel was going to attack Iran and that Washington had to be prepared to act in response.

Polls have suggested no candidate has a clear path to power. Israel’s prime minister is chosen through coalition-building in parliament rather than by direct popular vote.

“Netanyahu speaking to Americans, direct to camera, to justify this war and scold us about being upset about gas prices is a wildly disrespectful and super aggravating closing message,” the Democratic senator from Hawaii said in a post on X Sunday.
In his video message posted on social media, Netanyahu thanked Trump for the endorsement and said, “Israel has never had a greater friend in the White House”.
The remarks come as the US-Israeli war against Iran has contributed to declining public approval of both leaders, with their popularity falling to its lowest levels among the Israeli and American public.
The latest figures from the Pew Research Center, published on October 8, show that only 33% of Americans approve of Trump's handling of the U.S. military action against Iran, while 65% disapprove.

Trump Backs Netanyahu, Links Iran 'Finish the Job' to Vote
sources.text:
President Donald Trump endorsed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection on Sunday, nine days before Israelis vote, and attached to the endorsement a warning that went well beyond Israeli politics: if Israel chooses anyone else, he wrote, the United States "will have to do this work ourselves" against Iran.
The post on Truth Social ended weeks in which Trump had pointedly declined to pick a side. He had told Time magazine he would not say whether Israeli voters should give Netanyahu another term, said he did not "hear bad things" about the prime minister's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, and, as recently as Friday, told an interviewer, "I don't trust anybody." On Sunday the hedging was gone. "Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel," Trump wrote, describing Netanyahu as "Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself," and as "the kind of Partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel."
The passage that drew the most attention in Jerusalem and Tehran was the one about Iran. Trump wrote that the Islamic Republic had been "systematically destroyed, both militarily and financially," that the United States could "soon finish the job" unless Tehran changed its ways "rapidly," and that he might not want to if Israel's voters chose differently. "If Israel has the wrong leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves," he wrote. "BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!"
Asked by Axios later Sunday why he had waited, Trump said he had always intended to endorse. "I just didn't want to do it too soon," he said. On whether he could work with a different Israeli leader: "Maybe I will, maybe I won't. Who wants to take the chance?"
Netanyahu responded within hours. "President Trump, my friend Donald — thank you for your extraordinary endorsement. Israel has never had a greater friend in the White House," he wrote on X. "Together we will never let Iran's regime get nuclear weapons." A second post, in Hebrew, promised that "together we will complete the mission." Defense Minister Israel Katz and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich welcomed the statement, and Likud's campaign began circulating it immediately. Israeli media reported that the prime minister's office had received no advance notice and found the post only after it was published on a platform the office does not use.
The timing was not accidental on the Israeli side either. Netanyahu had spent the weekend on American television, appearing on Fox News' "Life, Liberty & Levin" hours before the endorsement, and had told i24News on Saturday that an Eisenkot government would allow Iran to obtain nuclear weapons. On Sunday he said he had instructed Israel's security agencies to pursue the fall of the Islamic Republic itself. The endorsement arrived with the campaign's central argument already in place: that only the Netanyahu-Trump partnership can finish the war that the two men started together on Feb. 28.
Eisenkot, the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces whose centrist Yashar party has led Likud in most recent polls, answered from a conference at Tel Aviv University. "I admire Trump," he said, "but Israel is a democratic country: only Israelis can choose their leader." On Channel 12 that evening he went further, saying he had asked the administration not to intervene. "I requested that there be no intervention in Israel's internal election," he said, acknowledging "a number of meetings" with Trump officials that he declined to describe. Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who leads the B'Yachad party and is also running to replace Netanyahu, said Trump's choice would not prevent cooperation with a different government. "Ultimately, in international politics, every leader works with the leader who is elected," he said.
Whether the endorsement moves votes is an open question in Israel, where American presidents have generally avoided declaring for a candidate even when their preferences were obvious. The nearest precedent is Bill Clinton's visible support for Shimon Peres in 1996, an election Peres lost to a first-time candidate named Benjamin Netanyahu. Polls published before Sunday showed Yashar ahead of Likud, in one survey by 22 seats to 18 in the 120-member Knesset, and betting markets had Eisenkot as the favorite to form the next government. Trump's approval among Israelis is high, which is why Netanyahu wanted the endorsement; the risk, which Eisenkot's response was designed to exploit, is that voters resent being told by a foreign leader whom to choose.
The endorsement is also a reversal in tone from a relationship that has been strained for much of the war. Trump criticized Israel's strike on an Iranian gas field in the war's first weeks, called Netanyahu "crazy" in June and said he was "a little bit perturbed" that Israel's fighting with Hezbollah in Lebanon was holding back talks with Iran. Axios reported that in private conversations Trump has blamed Netanyahu for Israel's failure to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, attack, called him "his own worst enemy" and questioned whether he was damaging Israel's standing abroad. He has also repeatedly urged President Isaac Herzog to pardon Netanyahu in his long-running corruption trial. The decision to endorse anyway, Axios reported, was made earlier last week.
Tehran read the post as a threat and answered in kind. "Last time you wanted to 'finish the job,' Iran emerged even stronger," Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X. "Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs too." He added an accusation aimed at both leaders: "Netanyahu is driving America into another war to stay out of jail, whatever the consequences for Israel — let alone POTUS." Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said the armed forces had prepared "a more devastating plan than the 12- and 40-day wars" and that a new operational plan "will not proceed with rules that they know." He warned last week that undersea cables, data centers and artificial intelligence facilities worth $2 trillion would be "within range" if strikes resumed.
The same day, Iran's parliament confirmed Mehrdad Akhlaqi Ketabchi, a veteran of the country's aerospace and missile industries who is under U.S. and European Union sanctions, as defense minister, ending eight months of interim leadership since his predecessor was killed in the war's opening strikes. Akhlaqi told lawmakers Iran had taken steps to counter the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb that U.S. strike planning reportedly includes, and that the American president "should focus on ensuring his forces are withdrawn safely from our region."
Yet Araghchi, speaking in Baghdad, also said Iran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days remained on the table and that Tehran was reviewing American "comments" on it. If Washington accepted Iran's conditions, he said, the strait would be open within six days and talks would resume on the seventh. The United States has insisted that any negotiation address Iran's nuclear program from the start; Iran wants the strait first. Trump has said the strait is already open to everyone except Iran, and U.S. Central Command says 97 percent of ships seeking to transit have done so without being hit. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov was due in Tehran on Monday.
The endorsement therefore does two things at once. In Israel it converts an election that polls had framed as a referendum on Netanyahu into one that his campaign can frame as a referendum on the alliance with Washington. In the Iran war it signals, as Axios put it, that Trump is prepared to let Israel resume strikes after the Nov. 3 midterms — a timeline he set out himself on Oct. 8, when he said there would be no new strikes before the vote — provided Netanyahu is still in office to carry them out. Both readings were available on Sunday night, and both sides of the strait chose the one that served them.
What the endorsement cannot settle is the arithmetic. Israeli governments are formed by coalitions, not by the party that finishes first, and the bloc that has kept Netanyahu in power — Likud with the religious and far-right parties — has to reach 61 seats regardless of what the White House prefers. Eisenkot's and Bennett's responses were aimed less at Trump than at the undecided voters who will decide whether that bloc gets there. For Trump, the gamble is the reverse: having told Israelis that only one man can be trusted, he will have to work with whoever they choose on Oct. 27.

THE DAILY BS: HOW MUCH CAN YOU HANDLE?
SPARE ME THE BS (I’ve got things to do).
- President Trump endorsed Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday ahead of Israel’s October 27 election.
- Trump warned that choosing another Israeli leader could leave America with more responsibility for confronting Iran.
- Netanyahu welcomed the endorsement and promised that the two countries would complete their mission together.
LAY IT ON ME (I’ve got time).
Donald Trump has never been particularly interested in the diplomatic tradition of saying absolutely nothing while using the greatest possible number of words.
So when Israel’s election approached, Trump skipped the polite neutrality routine and delivered something much closer to a political ultimatum.
Reelect Benjamin Netanyahu, he told Israeli voters, or the United States could find itself doing the dirty work against Iran without the partner Trump believes it needs.
On Sunday, the president issued what he described as his “Complete and Total Endorsement” of Netanyahu, just nine days before Israel’s October 27 national election.
Trump praised the Israeli prime minister as “a Great Warrior Prime Minister” and “an even greater Partner for Peace” in the confrontation with Iran.
But the endorsement came with an unmistakable warning. “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump wrote.
That’s not exactly a subtle campaign advertisement.
Trump also praised Netanyahu’s resilience through years of intense opposition and political pressure. “Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant,” he wrote, arguing that the prime minister had become stronger under pressure.
Netanyahu responded appreciatively, thanking Trump for his support and declaring, “Together we will complete the mission!”
Trump’s endorsement comes after months of visible disagreements over strategy in the Middle East, and with Netanyahu confronting Israeli criticism over the October 7 catastrophe, the war and its aftermath.
Trump’s backing represents an important political intervention by an American president who remains popular among many Israeli voters.
Trump’s statement was not a formal announcement of a new American military commitment or withdrawal. It was a warning about what he believes Israeli leadership could mean for the continuing struggle with Iran.
Still, presidents rarely insert themselves into another democracy’s election quite this directly.
For Israelis deciding who should lead their country through the next chapter of the regional conflict, Trump has made his preference unmistakable.
He wants Bibi. He wants a dependable partner. And he doesn’t want Washington left holding the entire Iranian bag.

- Axios — Trump explains his endorsement in a phone interview

sources.news_title: Trump Endorses Netanyahu Days Before Election
sources.text:
With days to go before a crucial general election in Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu received a last-minute endorsement for re-election on Sunday from his longtime friend, U.S. President Donald Trump.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump posted on Truth Social Sunday. “Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel.”
It’s a ringing, albeit late, recommendation for someone Trump hasn’t seen eye-to-eye with in recent months over how Netanyahu’s government has navigated the Middle East conflict. Trump explained his delayed endorsement to Axios reporter Barak Ravid, saying that he’d always meant to endorse Netanyahu because they “have a good relationship, and because we’ll continue to do good things together.”
Trump said in his post that, if Israel were to have “the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi,” the U.S. would be left alone to face the Iran threat. The U.S. and Israel jointly struck Iran in late February, kickstarting a conflict that has not only upended global markets but also thrust Middle Eastern regional security into turmoil.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” Trump added, in apparent reference to Netanyahu’s domestic challenges, including a corruption trial, some of which the U.S. President has previously tried to influence. “Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived!”
Trump’s endorsement comes just before Israelis head to the polling booths on Oct. 27, some three years after the country’s war with terror group Hamas ignited. Since then, Netanyahu has been criticized by opponents for failing to deliver on his promise of restoring regional security.
Public disillusionment with Netanyahu was among several factors that led to the formation of the Yashar! (“Straight!”) Party, whose founder, former Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, is challenging Netanyahu for the premiership. Eisenkot’s son and nephews were killed in the war in the Gaza Strip.
It’s unclear how big of an electoral boost Netanyahu will get from Trump’s endorsement. An opinion poll from nonprofit The Jewish People Policy Institute in Jerusalem released this month shows that most Israelis still see Trump as a great friend of Israel. A separate opinion poll from JPPI, however, shows their trust in him has eroded. Eisenkot, reacting to Trump’s endorsement, said at an event in Tel Aviv that while he appreciates Trump, only Israelis will decide on their next Prime Minister. Some surveys show Yashar! is in a tight race with Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party.
Netanyahu nonetheless thanked his “dear friend Donald” in a video posted on social media, saying he was “honored” and “humbled” by Trump’s backing, adding that the U.S. was “fortunate” to have Trump as its leader in the fight to denuclearize Iran.
Trump and Netanyahu’s fraught friendship
Even before Trump became U.S. President, he had publicly endorsed Netanyahu, though Trump, still only a TV personality in 2013, said that the Israeli politician asked for it. Since Trump was first elected, the two have been political allies and friends. Their relationship, however, has seen a number of ups and downs since Trump returned to the White House last year.
Netanyahu was the first foreign leader invited to the White House during Trump’s second-term Administration, and he has met with Trump repeatedly since. Netanyahu pushed Trump to target three key Iranian nuclear facilities in June last year. Last November, Trump sent a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog, asking him to pardon Netanyahu on his drawn out corruption trial, which the U.S. President deemed to be “political, unjustified prosecution.”
On Feb. 11, when Trump and Netanyahu met in a closed-door meeting at the White House, Israel and the U.S. failed to reach an agreement on how to proceed with Iran. Netanyahu has long sought to decapitate the Iranian leadership, but Trump at the time insisted on negotiations. Netanyahu, nonetheless, reportedly pressed Trump to launch the Iran operation later that month.
Since their last meeting, their relationship has markedly shifted. Trump has since tried to find an off-ramp to the war in Iran, but Israel’s actions made such peace deal talks thorny.
In March, after Israel attacked Iran’s South Pars gas field in the Persian Gulf, Trump said he told Netanyahu to stop such attacks. Then, on April 17, Trump declared on Truth Social that Israel was “PROHIBITED” from further bombing Lebanon, where it was at war with the militant group Hezbollah. Netanyahu, however, insisted that Israeli troops would remain in southern Lebanon and that security threats persisted—complicating Washington’s efforts toward peace as Tehran indicated that any deal would need to include a halt of the attacks in Lebanon.
When Netanyahu in June ordered strikes on a Hezbollah stronghold in Beirut to retaliate against the group’s alleged attacks on Israel, Trump phoned and excoriated the Israeli Prime Minister, reportedly calling him “f-cking crazy.” Asked by CNBC about the call, Netanyahu said: “We have common goals. Sometimes we have, as in the best of families, you have these tactical disagreements. We always find a way to work them out, and we do so as great friends.”
During Netanyahu’s seventh U.S. visit in July, Trump went public with his frustration. During a telephone interview on Fox News, Trump criticized Netanyahu over reports that the Israeli leader planned to share intelligence showing Iran rebuilding its nuclear program. The U.S. President said: “I don’t need Bibi to tell me that. Bibi is telling me that because he wants me to stay involved.”
Netanyahu is part of Trump’s U.N. alternative called the Board of Peace, though Israel broke again with the U.S. President by rejecting having Turkish and Qatari representatives on the board’s subpanel, the Gaza Executive Board, which is tasked with overseeing post-war reconstruction in the Gaza Strip.
Then Netanyahu rejected the Board of Peace’s 15-point plan to advance a cease-fire in the Gaza Strip and insisted that Israel would not withdraw before Hamas fully disarmed.
In Trump’s extensive interview with TIME in late September, Trump did not answer directly when asked repeatedly if the Israeli population should give Netanyahu another term. “I can only say that I’m not involved in politics anymore,” the U.S. President said.
But despite the lack of clear endorsement then, Trump seemed confident that “Bibi” could still win. “People have written off Bibi many, many times, just like they’ve written off me many, many times,” Trump told TIME. “I wouldn’t underestimate Bibi.”

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — President Trump on Sunday endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu late in his reelection campaign, a coveted boost because of Trump’s popularity but one that the American had withheld for months as the vote neared and the leaders’ strategies in the Middle East diverged.
Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu “has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran.”
Israelis are set to vote Oct. 27, in the first national elections since Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
The absence of an endorsement was a setback for the Likud politician, who had billed his tight ties to the Republican president as a selling point for staying in power.
“Thank you, President Trump, for the tremendous support and work together,” Netanyahu said in a statement in Hebrew posted on X. “Together we will complete the mission!”
His Likud Party attached to the statement a 35-second video showing clips of the two leaders together and Trump praising Netanyahu.
It was not immediately clear what impact the endorsement would have on what is expected to be a tight race. Trump is still popular in Israel, but many Israelis, including leading commentators, have expressed disappointment over the inconclusive outcome of the Iran war and Trump’s cease-fire proposal, which fell short of many of the countries’ key goals when they jointly launched the war in February.
In his post, Trump again threatened to “soon finish the job” against Iran “unless they change their ways, rapidly,” but added he might not want to if Netanyahu loses the election. “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump said.
He said Netanyahu had been “Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself.”
Trump endorsed Netanyahu in past elections and in November he sent a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog asking him to pardon Netanyahu on corruption charges.
But Trump’s comments about Netanyahu in recent months had been much more subdued, and he repeatedly demurred when asking if he would back the prime minister. The president, when asked in a Time magazine interview published this month about backing the Israeli leader, said, “I’m not involved in politics anymore,” despite his campaigning for and endorsing US politicians.
Trump, especially in his second term, has sought to give his stamp of approval to candidates in foreign elections and claimed credit when they have been successful. He endorsed Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in his unsuccessful bid for a fifth term, as well as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Polish President Karol Nawrocki, and several Latin American leaders.
Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies and seemed more aligned than ever in the wake of the joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities in 2025. But over the course of the nearly eight-month war with Iran this year, they have had disagreements.
Trump criticized Israel’s decision to attack a key Iranian gas field in the first weeks of the war. In June, he called Netanyahu “crazy.” Trump also said that he was “a little bit perturbed” as Israel’s fighting with Hezbollah militants in Lebanon was holding back peace talks with Iran.
Beyond Iran, Netanyahu in August rejected Trump’s latest plan to advance a stalled ceasefire in Gaza, pushing back on the US administration’s call for Israel to withdraw from territory it controls in Gaza until Hamas has been disarmed.

sources.text:
JERUSALEM, Oct 19 — US President Donald Trump endorsed his ally Benjamin Netanyahu yesterday ahead of Israel’s closely fought parliamentary election on Oct 27, giving the veteran prime minister a boost in his bid for a new mandate.
Netanyahu touted his close relationship with the US president in a video released by his Likud party, saying that together they had “crushed Iran” and that re-election would allow him to work with Trump to “eliminate the Iranian threat over the next two years, or even sooner”.
The endorsement comes less than two weeks before Israel’s first election since the Oct 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack, for which opposition politicians have accused Netanyahu of bearing personal responsibility after allegedly ignoring warnings.
Trump and Netanyahu, who polls show is in a tight election race, have worked closely together on Israel’s multi-front wars following the Hamas-led attack, including strikes on Iran. The endorsement could bolster Netanyahu’s re-election campaign.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, using a common nickname for the Israeli leader.
“This is the kind of Partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel, a Country for which it has done so much. Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel.”
The election is seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, who quickly thanked the US leader for his support yesterday.
“Thank you, President Trump, for your tremendous support and for our work together. Together we will complete the mission!” he wrote on X.
“I ask you to listen carefully to what President Trump said this evening,” Netanyahu told voters. “He said that together we have accomplished extraordinary things... But there is still a mission to complete.”
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned that Netanyahu was “driving America into another war”.
“Last time you wanted to ‘finish the job’, Iran emerged even stronger. Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs too,” Araghchi wrote on X.
Trump joined Netanyahu in a US-Israeli attack on Iran in late February but agreed to a ceasefire in April amid widespread US public opposition to the war, which had sent oil prices spiralling.
Speaking at an event in August, Netanyahu said Trump “is our greatest friend, one of the greatest friends we have had in the White House”.
But relations between the two have at times been strained over Iran, with Netanyahu saying no diplomatic agreement was possible with Iran’s leadership while Trump sought a negotiated end to the months-long conflict.
Voter warning
The endorsement comes after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned of a brewing “crisis” in the occupied West Bank after an American photojournalist for The Washington Post was injured in a brutal attack by Israeli settlers.
“We’re very disturbed by those images and what we’re seeing,” Rubio told reporters on Saturday. Netanyahu’s office said it was investigating the circumstances surrounding the attack.
With Israel and Netanyahu looking increasingly isolated on the world stage, Trump’s support is vital.
Netanyahu, who turns 77 on Oct 21, is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, having served on and off for more than 19 years.
The wily political operator returned to power in December 2022, bringing in once-shunned ultra-nationalists and quickly trying to rein in the judiciary, which is examining corruption charges that could land him in jail.
His main election rival is opposition politician Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the centre-right Yashar party and a former military chief who regularly accuses Netanyahu of bearing personal responsibility for the Oct 7 attack.
About seven million Israelis will be eligible to vote in the legislative election.
Current polls show that neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the one led by Eisenkot is in a position to win the 61 seats needed to control the 120-seat parliament and form a governing coalition.
Eisenkot said only Israelis could choose who they wanted to run the country.
Speaking at a conference in Tel Aviv, Eisenkot said he “admires” Trump, “but Israel is a democratic country, only Israelis can choose their leaders”.
But Trump warned against Israel electing “anyone other than Bibi”, writing that if voters chose one of his rivals, “America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so”. — AFP

Trump's endorsement, posted Sunday morning, was addressed directly to Israeli voters and left no doubt about his preference. He added: "This is the kind of Partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel, a Country for which it has done so much."
Netanyahu responded on X shortly after, thanking the president and writing: "Thank you, President Trump, for the tremendous support and the joint work. Together, we will complete the mission."
The warning to Israeli voters was blunt: choose Netanyahu or risk fighting Iran without American help. "If Israel has the wrong leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump wrote, per The Jerusalem Post. PBS News noted that Israelis head to the polls October 27 in the first national elections since the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023.
The endorsement comes as no single bloc in Israel's 120-seat Knesset commands a majority. The 120-seat Knesset requires a coalition of at least 61 members to govern. Current forecasts show Likud winning roughly 18–22 seats, with a Netanyahu-aligned right-religious bloc projected at about 49–51 seats — short of a majority — leaving smaller parties with the balance of power, according to The Jerusalem Post. Israeli President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders after the vote before tapping a candidate to attempt coalition formation; Herzog is not on the ballot and does not lead a party.
The endorsement also landed as Iran-related tensions remain high. Iran International reported Sunday that IRGC deputy commander Mostafa Izadi claimed U.S. forces at sea have moved roughly 700 kilometers away to avoid Iranian missile range — an assertion that appeared in the IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency and could not be independently verified. The U.S. Virtual Embassy in Iran issued a security alert warning of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions.
Social media users amplified the endorsement quickly. X account @clashreport posted that Trump had given his "Complete and Total Endorsement" to Netanyahu, warning the U.S. would have to take on Iran itself if Israel chose another leader. Account @TrumpDailyPosts similarly described Trump calling Netanyahu a strong partner against Iran and warning that if Israel chooses the wrong leader, the United States may be left to act alone.
The endorsement drew attention from major outlets. The New York Times reported that Trump praised the embattled prime minister for his endurance and said any other candidate would be the "wrong Leader."

This is what an America First foreign policy looks like in practice: a U.S. president who tells the world plainly that American treasure and American lives will not be spent cleaning up other nations' political messes if they choose weak leadership. Trump is not meddling — he is stating the terms of the partnership. Israel gets the most capable wartime leader in its history, and America gets a partner who will finish the job against the Iranian regime rather than kick the can down the road for another administration.
The globalists and the legacy media will call this interference. They said the same thing when Trump moved the embassy to Jerusalem and brokered the Abraham Accords. The reality is simpler: the Biden administration spent four years funding Iran's proxies and loosening sanctions, and now Trump is making clear that strength — not appeasement — is what keeps the Middle East from burning. If Israeli voters heed his warning, the mission against Tehran gets completed. If they don't, Americans should ask themselves why our sons and daughters would be asked to do a job Israel's own leaders refused to finish.

Trump’s endorsement has now placed the American president squarely in the middle of that choice, making the future of the U.S.-Israel alliance a central issue in Israel’s approaching election.
Whether Israeli voters give Netanyahu another mandate remains uncertain. But the prime minister has made his message unmistakable: the next two years could determine whether Israel completes its campaign against Iran’s regional threat or leaves unfinished business for a potentially less favorable political era.

Trump's late backing comes as the two leaders’ strategies on Iran and Gaza have diverged, and he warns the US may not “do this work” if Israel changes leaders.
US President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the final stretch of his reelection campaign.
The endorsement is a coveted boost given Trump’s popularity in Israel, but one he withheld for months as the vote approached and the two leaders’ strategies in the Middle East diverged.
In a post on social media, Trump said that Netanyahu “has been a great warrior prime minister and an even greater partner for peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran.”
Israelis are set to vote on 27 October in the first national elections since Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023.
“Thank you, President Trump, for the tremendous support and work together,” Netanyahu said in a Hebrew-language statement on X. “Together we will complete the mission!”
The lack of an endorsement had been a blow to the Likud party politician, who has billed his close ties to Trump as a selling point for staying in power.
Likud attached a 35-second video to the statement, showing clips of the two leaders together and Trump praising Netanyahu.
It is not yet clear what impact the endorsement will have on a race expected to be tight.
The absence of an endorsement was a setback for the Likud politician, who had billed his tight ties to the Republican president as a selling point for staying in power.
Trump's endorsement comes after months of reticence
Trump has backed Netanyahu in past elections, and in November he wrote to Israeli President Isaac Herzog asking him to pardon Netanyahu on corruption charges.
In recent months, however, Trump’s remarks about the prime minister had been far more subdued, and he repeatedly demurred when asked whether he would support him.
Asked about it in a Time magazine interview published this month, Trump said, “I’m not involved in politics anymore,” even though he continues to campaign for and endorse US politicians.
Trump remains popular in Israel; however, many Israelis, including leading commentators, have voiced disappointment over the inconclusive outcome of the Iran war and over Trump’s ceasefire proposal, which fell short of many of the key goals the two countries had set when they jointly launched the war in February.
In his post on Sunday, Trump again threatened to “soon finish the job” against Iran “unless they change their ways rapidly." He added that he might not want to if Netanyahu loses.
“If Israel has the wrong leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump said.
He described Netanyahu as “strong, brave, and brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel itself.”
Trump and Netanyahu have long been close allies and appeared more aligned than ever after the joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities in 2025. Over the course of the nearly eight-month war with Iran this year, however, they have clashed.
Trump criticised Israel’s decision to attack a key Iranian gas field in the first weeks of the war. In June he called Netanyahu "crazy", and he said he was “a little bit perturbed” that Israel’s fighting with Hezbollah militants in Lebanon was holding back peace talks with Iran.
On Gaza, Netanyahu in August rejected Trump’s latest plan to advance a stalled ceasefire. The plan called for Israel to withdraw from territory it controls in Gaza before Hamas has been disarmed, and Netanyahu pushed back on it.
Especially in his second term, Trump has sought to put his stamp of approval on candidates in foreign elections claiming credit when they win.
He endorsed Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in his unsuccessful bid for a fifth term, as well as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Polish President Karol Nawrocki and several Latin American leaders.

Trump Endorses Netanyahu as Israeli Rivals Reject Foreign Intervention
By The Media Line Staff
US President Donald Trump endorsed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection Sunday, October 18, nine days before Israel’s parliamentary election, prompting opposition leaders Gadi Eisenkot and Naftali Bennett to insist that Israeli voters alone would determine the country’s next government.
President Trump announced his “Complete and Total Endorsement” on Truth Social, praising Netanyahu’s leadership during Israel’s confrontation with Iran and describing him as a trusted American partner.
“If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi,” President Trump warned, the United States could face additional military responsibilities against Iran.
Netanyahu thanked the US president for his support, declaring, “Together we will complete the mission!”
Speaking at an election conference at Tel Aviv University, Eisenkot, chairman of the centrist Yashar party, rejected outside involvement.
“Israel’s citizens are the only ones who will decide who the prime minister will be,” he said.
Eisenkot subsequently told Channel 12 that he had sought to prevent the endorsement. “I requested that there be no intervention in Israel’s internal election. But I’ll deal with it.”
He also questioned whether renewed military action against Iran was necessary before the election and repeated his demand for a state commission investigating the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack.
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, leader of the B’Yachad party, said President Trump’s support for Netanyahu would not prevent cooperation with another Israeli government.
“Ultimately, in international politics, every leader works with the leader who is elected,” Bennett said.
Bennett called for cooperation between Israel’s Zionist left and right and insisted he remained a candidate for prime minister.
Separately, National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir claimed Netanyahu had privately promised European officials to exclude his Otzma Yehudit party from the next government. Likud rejected the accusation, calling it a political fabrication.
President Trump’s intervention departs from the traditional diplomatic convention that national leaders avoid openly supporting candidates in allied democracies. Such endorsements are not automatically unlawful, but they raise questions about foreign interference and national sovereignty.
In 2019, President Trump publicly supported Netanyahu’s leadership, although the White House explicitly denied endorsing him during that year’s election campaign.
The US president has subsequently backed foreign political leaders more openly, including Hungary’s Viktor Orbán and Argentina’s Javier Milei.
Recent Israeli polls place Eisenkot’s party ahead of Likud, although neither major political bloc appears assured of the 61 Knesset seats needed for a governing majority. Under Israel’s parliamentary system, coalition negotiations, rather than the largest party’s vote total alone, determine who becomes prime minister.

Trump endorses Netanyahu in close Israeli election
WASHINGTON/TEL AVIV >> President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed his ally Benjamin Netanyahu as the longtime Israeli prime minister struggles for an edge in next week’s parliamentary election.
Trump praised Netanyahu as a “great warrior prime minister” and peace partner, crediting him with joining the United States in launching strikes on Iran in February. The conflict, in its seventh month, has disrupted energy markets globally and wreaked havoc across the Middle East, damaging critical infrastructure and destabilizing regional economies.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.
“Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived! I have watched Bibi under the most trying of times. Normal men or women in such situations would have wilted under the pressure — But Bibi did not wilt, he actually got stronger, and maintains that same Strength today.”
In his message, addressed to “the Great People of Israel,” Trump added, “Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel.”
The Trump endorsement is not certain to give Netanyahu and his right-wing Likud party a boost in the October 27 national election, as Israeli public support for Trump has diminished amid Israeli-US disagreements over Iran.

Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
Polls have suggested no candidate has a clear path to power. Israel’s prime minister is chosen through coalition-building in parliament rather than by direct popular vote.
It will be Israel’s first vote since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil, as Israel went to war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
The election could determine whether Netanyahu remains in power after one of the most consequential periods in Israel’s history, or is defeated by centrist rivals promising to usher in a new era.
Netanyahu promptly expressed his thanks to his “dear friend Donald” on X, saying, “Together we will complete the mission!”
Trump has broken with longtime US tradition by endorsing candidates in elections in foreign countries including Hungary, Colombia, Argentina, Japan and Honduras.
Endorsement might help, can’t hurt
Trump’s relationship with Netanyahu has been close but also fractious, with the president at times publicly and privately criticizing Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.
The war that the US and Israel launched against Iran is unpopular with Americans, who vote November 3 in congressional elections, while support for Israel among Americans has also decreased over the Iran war and Israel’s conduct in the three-year war in Gaza that Trump has promised to end. Both leaders on Sunday mentioned finishing the job in Iran.
Tamar Hermann, a senior research fellow at the non-partisan Israel Democracy Institute in Jerusalem, said Trump’s late endorsement could help win back wavering Netanyahu voters but was unlikely to draw widespread support.
Most Israelis, even those who are critical of Netanyahu and his government, were largely in favor of the Iran war.
In an election this close, “it couldn’t hurt him, and it might help,” said analyst Aaron David Miller of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Washington.
Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, although the opposition may also struggle to form a government, opinion polls show. That could lead to Netanyahu serving as a caretaker prime minister while another election is held.
The U.S. president passed up earlier opportunities to endorse Netanyahu, perhaps because he wanted to see what leverage he could exercise on issues like Gaza or Lebanon, said Miller. In the end, he said, Trump sided with a leader he sees as strong and unfairly persecuted.
“However angry Trump may be at Netanyahu for pushing this Iran war, this in the end was a Trump decision,” Miller added.
A Trump decision not to endorse Netanyahu would have raised “legitimate questions about whether or not the whole Iran venture was in fact something Trump should have done,” he said.

President Trump Endorses Netanyahu Ahead of Israeli Election, Warns America Could Be Left to Confront Iran Alone
President Trump has thrown his full support behind Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s October 27 parliamentary elections, praising the longtime leader’s handling of Iran and warning that a change in leadership could leave the United States carrying a greater burden in the Middle East.
The president announced his endorsement Sunday in a lengthy Truth Social post addressed directly to the Israeli people, ending months of uncertainty about whether he would publicly support Netanyahu’s reelection campaign.
Trump described Netanyahu as a strong wartime leader and an important American partner in confronting the Iranian regime.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace,” Trump wrote, emphasizing their cooperation against Iran.
The president credited Netanyahu with standing alongside the United States during the military campaign launched against Iran in February, arguing that their combined efforts had significantly weakened Tehran’s military and financial capabilities.
Trump also warned that Iran could face additional military action unless its leadership changes course.
The president’s endorsement comes just nine days before Israeli voters head to the polls in an election that will determine whether Netanyahu can assemble another governing coalition.
Trump made clear that he considers Netanyahu’s continued leadership important to American interests, particularly as Washington confronts ongoing security threats from Iran.
“If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump declared.
The warning reflects the president’s position that Israel should remain an active partner in confronting regional threats rather than placing additional military responsibilities on American forces.
Trump also praised Netanyahu for remaining in office despite years of political controversy and pressure from opponents inside Israel.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” the president wrote.
He argued that the Israeli prime minister had endured significant challenges while continuing to pursue his government’s security objectives.
Trump concluded his message by giving Netanyahu his complete endorsement for another term as prime minister.
The announcement immediately drew a response from Netanyahu, who thanked the American president for his backing and their work together.
“Together we will complete the mission!” Netanyahu wrote on X.
The endorsement represents an important development in the relationship between the two leaders, who have maintained close political ties despite occasional disagreements over military operations and diplomatic negotiations.
Trump had previously declined to endorse Netanyahu when questioned about the Israeli election, leaving open the possibility that he might remain neutral in the contest.
As recently as Thursday, the president avoided committing himself to a candidate.
His Sunday announcement ended that uncertainty and placed the White House firmly behind Netanyahu’s reelection effort.
The decision comes during a particularly difficult period for Israel, which continues confronting the consequences of the October 7, 2023, Hamas terrorist attacks and the wars that followed.
The upcoming election will be Israel’s first national parliamentary vote since those attacks, which killed approximately 1,200 people and resulted in hundreds being taken hostage.
Netanyahu’s government has faced questions about the security failures preceding the assault, the subsequent military campaign in Gaza and the broader regional conflict.
The Israeli prime minister has maintained that his government must prioritize the country’s security and prevent hostile organizations and governments from rebuilding their military capabilities.
Iran has remained central to that strategy.
In February, American and Israeli forces launched coordinated strikes against Iranian targets, beginning a conflict that has continued to disrupt the region.
The initial operations killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and targeted military installations and other facilities associated with Tehran’s defense infrastructure.
Trump has repeatedly defended the campaign as necessary to confront threats posed by Iran.
However, the conflict has also created economic consequences, particularly through disruptions to international energy markets.
Rising fuel prices have become an issue in the United States as the administration seeks to contain the economic effects of the fighting.
The war has also generated disagreements between Washington and Jerusalem over the timing and scope of military operations.
Earlier this year, Trump expressed frustration with Netanyahu during discussions about Israeli operations involving Hezbollah in Lebanon.
The president was reportedly concerned that continued military escalation could interfere with diplomatic efforts involving Iran.
Despite those disagreements, Sunday’s endorsement demonstrates that Trump continues to regard Netanyahu as a valuable security partner.
Israel’s election is being contested by several political parties, with Netanyahu’s Likud party seeking enough parliamentary support to form another government.
Among the major challengers is Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief whose Yashar party has emerged as a significant competitor.
Israeli governments are formed through parliamentary coalitions, meaning the largest party does not automatically secure the prime minister’s office.
A coalition must command the support of at least 61 members of Israel’s 120-seat Knesset.
Recent polling has indicated that neither Netanyahu’s existing coalition nor the opposition has a guaranteed parliamentary majority, leaving the composition of the next government uncertain.
Trump’s endorsement arrives as the parties enter the final stretch of campaigning.
The president remains popular among significant portions of the Israeli public, particularly voters who value his administration’s military and diplomatic support for Israel.
His decision to intervene publicly also underscores the importance Washington places on the outcome of the election.
During Trump’s first presidency, the United States recognized Jerusalem as Israel’s capital, moved the American embassy there and recognized Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights.
His administration also helped negotiate the Abraham Accords, which established diplomatic normalization agreements between Israel and several Arab countries.
Those achievements became defining elements of the relationship between Trump and Netanyahu.
The two leaders have continued working together during Trump’s second term, particularly on security matters involving Iran.
Nevertheless, the upcoming election remains a decision for Israeli voters, who will determine the makeup of the Knesset and the possibilities for forming a new government.
Trump has now made his preference unmistakable.
With the election scheduled for October 27, the president is publicly backing Netanyahu while warning that a change in Israeli leadership could complicate American efforts to confront Iran and maintain security cooperation in the Middle East.

sources.news_title: How much will Trump’s endorsement help Netanyahu?
sources.text:
How much will Trump’s endorsement help Netanyahu?
“This is the first time ever that the president, at least publicly, endorses a candidate in Israel’s election.”
(JTA) — JERUSALEM – Within minutes of President Donald Trump endorsing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a post on Truth Social Sunday, Netanyahu’s campaign team had released a 30-second clip showing all the times Trump has lavished praise on the Israeli leader over the past few years.
With polls showing that Netanyahu and his governing coalition are slipping in their struggle to retain power in the upcoming Oct. 27 election and lag behind the opposition bloc, an endorsement from the president of the United States is a powerful statement.
But is it enough to tip the scales?
“I don’t think it will change anything,” said Ilana Shpaizman, a senior lecturer in the Department of Political Studies at Bar-Ilan University.
Of course, she said, “Netanyahu will say this is the proof that I’m a leader and all that, and I can speak to Trump … But so what? His followers already know that and they believe in him. They don’t need the endorsement.”
Those who oppose him, Shpaizman continued, “know that Trump forced him (Netanyahu) to accept the ceasefire in Gaza and accept the hostage deal, and that Trump runs the show around Iran. So they also don’t need the endorsement either,” Shpaizman said.
Some pundits speaking on Israeli news outlets criticized Trump for “interfering” in Israel’s election, while others put it down to the fact that Trump does not want America to return to fighting Iran alone if Netanyahu, who is hawkish on Iran, is replaced by someone less willing to act militarily. If Netanyahu loses, that is a scenario that could play out.
“This is the first time ever that the president, at least publicly, endorses a candidate in Israel’s election,” Bushinsky, a political commentator and former adviser to Netanyahu, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.
Bushinsky said he remembered Netanyahu complaining about U.S. intervention in previous elections in 1999 and 2001, when presidents less enamored of him were in office. He even pushed for an initiative that would block foreign funding for election campaigns.
Now, Bushinsky said, “I guess he is not complaining,” adding that the endorsement serves Netanyahu in two ways.
First, it signals that Trump thinks that Netanyahu is the most suitable guy for the job. Second, it puts Netanyahu’s election campaign back on track, refocusing attention on an issue where Netanyahu is strong – Iran.
“It lets him say ‘I can now finish a job, and I can finish a job with Trump,’ and ‘without Trump or without me, the job will not be finished,’” said Bushinsky.
He said that in the last few days, the political debate had pivoted to other issues such as Ashkenazim vs Sephardim, the draft law and the contentious efforts by the outgoing government to overhaul the judiciary.
“This [endorsement] is the ultimate campaign boost for Netanyahu,” Bushinsky said.
But that boost might not be enough.
Most of the polls taken in recent days show the opposition bloc led by former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot pulling ahead of Netanyahu’s ruling coalition, but give neither bloc enough seats to gain the necessary 61 of 120 seats in Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, to form the next government.
“I think this might give Netanyahu one more seat, one more mandate, but not more than that,” said Bushinsky.
Prof. Tamar Hermann, director of the Israel Democracy Institute’s Viterbi Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research, said that the timing of Trump’s support for Netanyahu in this election race had come both “too late and too early.”
“It’s too late because people have already decided electoral preferences. They may shift within each bloc, but will not move between the blocs because of this,” she said. “And it’s too early because there are nine days to go to the elections, and we can already see other American leaders spilling some cold water over what he said, even on the Republican side of the aisle.”
This criticism, Hermann continued, will be transmitted to Israeli voters, and they will see that Trump is facing a huge battle in the upcoming midterm elections.
“The image of President Trump has deteriorated significantly since April 26, when he started the negotiations with Iran,” she said, pointing to one of the IDI’s recent public opinion surveys that found the president’s popularity had plummeted after he stopped the war with Iran without totally removing the threats against the State of Israel.
According to that poll, the Israeli public’s confidence in Trump as someone dedicated to Israel’s security fell from around 70% to just 42%.
“In my view, the endorsement will not make a big change,” Hermann added. “It will just strengthen Netanyahu’s political supporters, who will see it as a sign that he is still the internationally known figure that even the president of the United States is endorsing.”
She concluded, “The meaning of endorsement in Israel is totally different than in the United States … we are not that used to this kind of move, and it will not make people change their minds.”

US President Donald Trump has urged Israelis to vote for Benjamin Netanyahu in the nation's coming election.
Mr Netanyahu seized on the endorsement, writing on social media: "A friend of Israel wants Netanyahu to win."
Just months ago, the US president unleashed an expletive-laden tirade against Mr Netanyahu.
US President Donald Trump has written a glowing endorsement of the Israeli prime minister just months after labelling him "crazy" and days after suggesting he does not trust him.
In a lengthy post on his Truth Social platform, Mr Trump urged Israelis to vote for Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party in their upcoming election, now just over a week away.
He labelled the Israeli prime minister a "Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace", pointing to the decision the pair took to launch their war against Iran on February 28.
Negotiations to end that conflict have been stalled for months, despite Mr Trump's repeated insistence Iran has been defeated.
"If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," he wrote.
"Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself.

He said Mr Netanyahu was the partner the US was "demanding of Israel, a Country for which it has done so much".
"Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel," Mr Trump said.
Mr Netanyahu seized upon the endorsement, posting an image on social media showing Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas, Iran's reclusive Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani along with the caption: "Israel's enemies want Netanyahu to lose."
It was accompanied by an image of the Israeli prime minister and Mr Trump, and the caption: "A friend of Israel wants Netanyahu to win."
Trump changes tune
In June, the US president unleashed an expletive-laden tirade against Mr Netanyahu as he effectively accused him of trying to undermine the prospects of a deal with Iran.
During a fiery phone call, after the Israeli prime minister ordered strikes on central Beirut against Iranian-backed Hezbollah, Mr Trump said Mr Netanyahu was "f***ing crazy" and said he would be in jail had it not been for his efforts to protect him.
Mr Netanyahu is subject to an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court (ICC) for alleged war crimes — something the US has condemned the court for pursuing, issuing sanctions against its officials in response.
The Israeli prime minister is also embroiled in a long-running corruption case at home, which is still before the local courts.
Mr Trump has previously urged Israeli President Isaac Herzog to pardon the prime minister, which he has to this point refused to do.
On Friday, during an interview with US network Newsmax, Mr Trump talked up the success of his relationship with Mr Netanyahu.

The relationship between the US and Israel, and their leaders, has been a focus of campaigning during the election, with some of Mr Netanyahu's opponents accusing him of weakening the ties with Israel's closest ally.
Reports emerged earlier this month that the Trump administration had encouraged Israel to launch unilateral attacks against Iran, shattering the relative calm that had persisted for months, because the US president did not want to return to all-out war before the US midterm elections in November.

In an unusually direct intervention in Israeli politics, Trump posted a letter on Truth Social to “the Great People of Israel” offering his “Complete and Total Endorsement” of Netanyahu ahead of the elections later this month.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting [sic] the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump wrote, using Netanyahu’s nickname.
Trump warned that Iran, which has long threatened to destroy Israel and the US, had been severely weakened by their joint military campaign but could face further attacks unless it changed course.
“If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” he said.
Trump praised Netanyahu for resisting pressure during nearly eight months of regional conflict, including opposition from within Israel.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself. Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived!” Trump wrote.
“I have watched Bibi under the most trying of times,” he continued. “Normal men or women in such situations would have wilted under the pressure — But Bibi did not wilt, he actually got stronger, and maintains that same Strength today. This is the kind of Partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel, a Country for which it has done so much.”
Trump concluded his message with an emphatic assurance to Israeli voters: “BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!”
The endorsement came after months in which Trump had conspicuously declined to back Netanyahu, despite repeated questions about the Israeli election and the prime minister’s emphasis on his close relationship with the American president.
In a telephone interview with Axios on Sunday, Trump said the timing had been deliberate.
“I was always going to do that. I just didn’t want to do it too soon,” he told veteran journalist Barak Ravid.
Trump stressed his good relationship with Netanyahu, saying, “It is important that Israel has a person they can count on.”
Asked whether he could work with a different Israeli leader, Trump declined to offer an assurance.
“Maybe I will, maybe I won’t. Who wants to take the chance?” he said.

In an interview with Israel’s Channel 14 later Sunday, Netanyahu described Trump’s support as personally gratifying and argued that their relationship was an important strategic asset for Israel.
The prime minister urged voters to consider which Israeli leader would be capable of working with Trump during the remaining two years of his presidency, particularly in confronting regional threats and expanding the Abraham Accords, the normalization agreements between Israel and several Arab countries.
Netanyahu questioned whether his leading challenger, former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, possessed the diplomatic experience or capabilities necessary to work with the American administration.
Eisenkot, who heads the centrist Yashar party and has emerged as Netanyahu’s principal challenger, said he respected Trump but rejected the suggestion that the US president should influence Israel’s choice of leader.
He insisted that Israel’s election was a domestic matter and that Israeli citizens alone would determine the next government.
“I have great respect for the president; he is a great friend of Israel. But the elections in Israel are an internal Israeli matter, and the only ones who will decide are the citizens of Israel,” he told Israel’s Channel 12 news.
Asked whether he had tried to prevent Trump’s endorsement, Eisenkot said there had been several meetings that he did not wish to discuss in detail, and that he had specifically requested that the US president refrain from intervening in Israel’s election.
Eisenkot separately addressed the possibility of renewed fighting against Iran, saying he was not aware of intelligence requiring urgent military action before the election. He expressed confidence in IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir to assess any immediate threat.

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — President Trump on Sunday endorsed beleaguered Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu late in his reelection campaign, a coveted boost because of Trump’s popularity in Israel but one that the American had withheld for months as the vote neared and the leaders’ strategies for the Middle East diverged.
Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu “has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran.”
Israelis are set to vote Oct. 27, in the first national elections since Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
The absence of an endorsement was a setback for the prime minister, who had billed his close ties to the U.S. president as a selling point for staying in power.
“Thank you, President Trump, for the tremendous support and work together,” Netanyahu said in a statement in Hebrew posted on X. “Together we will complete the mission!”
His Likud Party attached to the statement a 35-second video showing clips of the two leaders together and Trump praising Netanyahu.
It was not immediately clear what impact the endorsement would have on what is expected to be a tight race. Trump is still popular in Israel, but many Israelis, including leading commentators, have expressed disappointment over the inconclusive outcome of the Iran war and Trump’s ceasefire proposal, which fell short of many of the countries’ key goals when they jointly launched the war in February.
In his post, Trump again threatened to “soon finish the job” against Iran “unless they change their ways, rapidly,” but added he might not want to if Netanyahu loses the election. “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump said.
He said Netanyahu had been “Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself.”
Trump endorsed Netanyahu in past elections, and in November he sent a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog asking him to pardon Netanyahu on corruption charges.
But Trump’s comments about Netanyahu in recent months had been much more subdued, and he repeatedly demurred when asking if he would back the prime minister. The president, when asked in a Time magazine interview published this month about backing the Israeli leader, said, ”I’m not involved in politics anymore,” despite his campaigning for and endorsing U.S. politicians.
Trump, especially in his second term, has sought to give his stamp of approval to candidates in foreign elections and claimed credit when they have been successful. He endorsed Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in his unsuccessful bid for a fifth term, as well as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Polish President Karol Nawrocki — both of whom were elected — and several Latin American leaders.
Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies and seemed more aligned than ever in the wake of the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities in 2025. But over the course of the nearly eight-month war with Iran this year, they have had disagreements.
Trump criticized Israel’s decision to attack a key Iranian gas field in the first weeks of the war. In June, he called Netanyahu “crazy.” Trump also said that he was “a little bit perturbed” as Israel’s fighting with Hezbollah militants in Lebanon was holding back peace talks with Iran.
Beyond Iran, Netanyahu in August rejected Trump’s latest plan to advance a stalled ceasefire in the Gaza Strip, dismissing the U.S. administration’s call for Israel to withdraw from territory it controls in Gaza until Hamas has been disarmed.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu late in his re-election campaign, a coveted boost because of Trump’s popularity but one that the American had withheld for months as the vote neared and the leaders’ strategies in the Middle East diverged.
Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu “has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran.”
Israelis are set to vote Oct. 27, in the first national elections since Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
The absence of an endorsement was a setback for the Likud politician, who had billed his tight ties to the Republican president as a selling point for staying in power.
“Thank you, President Trump, for the tremendous support and work together,” Netanyahu said in a statement in Hebrew posted on X. “Together we will complete the mission!”
His Likud Party attached to the statement a 35-second video showing clips of the two leaders together and Trump praising Netanyahu.

It was not immediately clear what impact the endorsement would have on what is expected to be a tight race. Trump is still popular in Israel, but many Israelis, including leading commentators, have expressed disappointment over the inconclusive outcome of the Iran war and Trump’s ceasefire proposal, which fell short of many of the countries’ key goals when they jointly launched the war in February.
In his post, Trump again threatened to “soon finish the job” against Iran “unless they change their ways, rapidly,” but added he might not want to if Netanyahu loses the election. “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump said.
He said Netanyahu had been “Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself.”
Trump endorsed Netanyahu in past elections and in November he sent a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog asking him to pardon Netanyahu on corruption charges.
But Trump’s comments about Netanyahu in recent months had been much more subdued, and he repeatedly demurred when asking if he would back the prime minister. The president, when asked in a Time magazine interview published this month about backing the Israeli leader, said, “I’m not involved in politics any more,” despite his campaigning for and endorsing U.S. politicians.
Trump, especially in his second term, has sought to give his stamp of approval to candidates in foreign elections and claimed credit when they have been successful. He endorsed Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in his unsuccessful bid for a fifth term, as well as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Polish President Karol Nawrocki, and several Latin American leaders.
Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies and seemed more aligned than ever in the wake of the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities in 2025. But over the course of the nearly eight-month war with Iran this year, they have had disagreements.
Trump criticized Israel’s decision to attack a key Iranian gas field in the first weeks of the war. In June, he called Netanyahu “crazy.” Trump also said that he was “a little bit perturbed” as Israel’s fighting with Hezbollah militants in Lebanon was holding back peace talks with Iran.
Beyond Iran, Netanyahu in August rejected Trump’s latest plan to advance a stalled ceasefire in Gaza, pushing back on the U.S. administration’s call for Israel to withdraw from territory it controls in Gaza until Hamas has been disarmed.
